frictionVectors.title: European Gas Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over gas exports, but European buyers are pressing for pricing flexibility and expanded supply commitments. Infrastructure and contract negotiations remain key channels of external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases security costs and complicates Algeria's non-interventionist regional posture. Cross-border trafficking and militant mobility threaten remote energy corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal control of its petroleum sector but relies heavily on foreign capital, technology, and offshore operators to sustain production. Declining output and financing needs limit Luanda's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects remain important to national connectivity while creating long-term repayment and procurement sensitivities. Luanda is diversifying partners but cannot quickly replace established financing channels.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's role as a regional gateway gives Benin leverage, but trade flows remain sensitive to Nigerian policy and external logistics investment. Control over customs, rail, and road infrastructure is strategically important.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and insecurity along the northern frontier are increasing demands on state resources and threatening transport and extractive prospects. Foreign security assistance is useful but may constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana exercises unusually strong national influence over diamond production and revenue distribution, but remains exposed to global demand shifts and concentrated marketing channels. Synthetic diamonds add longer-term external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals could broaden the resource base while inviting competing foreign concessions. The main sovereignty challenge is securing local value addition rather than simply attracting extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is seeking greater state participation and domestic processing in gold, reducing the role of foreign operators. Production disruption, illicit mining, and limited technical capacity complicate efforts to convert resource nationalism into reliable revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from Western security partners toward Russia reflects a drive for strategic autonomy but creates dependence on a narrower external supplier. Security cooperation remains constrained by persistent militant violence and uncertain accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking to develop nickel and other mineral assets, but lacks the capital, processing capacity, and transport infrastructure to retain more value domestically. External investors and lenders therefore retain substantial leverage over project terms.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-border and aid pressure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent tensions with Rwanda and insecurity linked to eastern Congo constrain trade and regional infrastructure planning. Reduced or politically conditioned external assistance further narrows Bujumbura's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime-security competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's location supports partnerships with the United States, Europe, and other Atlantic actors in maritime security and logistics. This increases bargaining power but also exposes Praia to pressure over access, basing, and alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Connectivity-finance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy systems, and digital cables depend heavily on foreign investment and concessional finance. Debt sustainability and ownership of strategic infrastructure remain important safeguards for sovereign control.

highlights: Oil and gas remain state-finance anchors

frictionVectors.title: Resource-for-infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain central to roads, energy, and mining development, while opaque contracting can limit local value capture. Cameroon is attempting diversification, but transport and power bottlenecks preserve external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and pipeline risk
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten roads, agricultural production, and national cohesion. Security costs and instability complicate new extractive investment and weaken oversight of resource corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-minerals model
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has strengthened regime protection while increasing Moscow's influence over strategic sites and mining networks. This arrangement provides short-term security but reduces transparency and competitive state bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Road and export-corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and dependence on routes through Cameroon sharply limit the state's ability to tax and regulate gold, diamonds, and other commodities. Armed groups and informal operators continue to capture value along remote supply chains.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a fragile transition
Sahel and Sudan crises reshape alliances

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons remain the principal source of fiscal capacity, leaving Chad vulnerable to price shocks and external operators' technical and financial leverage. Limited domestic refining, transport, and processing capacity keeps value capture low.

frictionVectors.title: External security and corridor pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Sudan and the wider Sahel increases dependence on foreign security relationships and humanitarian infrastructure. Cross-border trade routes, refugee flows, and energy corridors are vulnerable to armed-group disruption and geopolitical competition.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros' territorial sovereignty and complicating relations with Paris. The dispute remains a recurring domestic and diplomatic pressure point.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support rely heavily on foreign donors, including France, Gulf partners, and multilateral lenders. This constrains policy autonomy despite diversified diplomatic outreach.

highlights: Eastern security crisis undermines state control

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains deeply connected to foreign firms, traders, and financing networks. Kinshasa is seeking stronger contract terms and local processing, but enforcement and transparency remain uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Conflict and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, cross-border networks, and regional security involvement continue to weaken government control over mineral-rich territories. Conflict-driven smuggling reduces public revenue and exposes infrastructure to political capture.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state remains highly dependent on oil exports and foreign technical and financial partners. Production volatility and limited diversification leave national resource control vulnerable to external market and creditor pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and industrial projects expand connectivity but can increase dependence on external contractors and financing. Debt sustainability and local value capture remain persistent concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Investment Concentration
frictionVectors.details: French, European, Chinese, and other foreign firms retain major positions in ports, telecoms, energy, and consumer infrastructure. Abidjan is improving regulation and bargaining power, but strategic sectors remain externally exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and Critical Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Cocoa exports generate substantial value while domestic processing and farmer incomes remain constrained. Port, energy, and transport expansion is strengthening sovereignty, though financing and technology still depend significantly on foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Military Base Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through foreign military facilities, including American, Chinese, French, and other presences. The revenue and security benefits are substantial, but strategic dependence and escalation risks limit sovereign maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, Debt, and Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: The country is central to Red Sea and Ethiopian trade routes, yet major port and rail assets have involved foreign operators and lenders. Debt exposure and operational dependence complicate Djibouti's ability to retain full control over its infrastructure strategy.

highlights: Gulf and IMF financing deepen dependence

frictionVectors.title: External financing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large IMF, Gulf, and other creditor commitments constrain policy autonomy and place strategic assets and state-linked enterprises under continuing scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains Egypt's central sovereignty and infrastructure risk, with negotiations vulnerable to regional escalation.

highlights: Gas monetization seeks a second life

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and dependence on foreign technical and commercial partners limit sovereign control over declining petroleum revenues.

frictionVectors.title: China-linked infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese construction and lending have expanded strategic infrastructure while reinforcing opaque debt, contracting, and repayment relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Mining partner dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects depend on foreign capital and operators, creating recurring concerns over revenue sharing, labor conditions, and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Instability around the Red Sea and neighboring Sudan and Ethiopia increases pressure from regional powers seeking ports, access, and security influence.

frictionVectors.title: South African dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South Africa for trade, transport, energy, finance, and imports, limiting independent control over critical supply routes.

frictionVectors.title: Trade-preference vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and textile industries remain exposed to changing regional and Western market-access rules, leaving jobs and foreign-exchange earnings vulnerable to external decisions.

highlights: Debt restructuring limits room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD has increased Ethiopia's control over domestic energy infrastructure but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan over filling and operations.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and investment conditionality
frictionVectors.details: External debt restructuring, IMF-backed reforms, and reliance on foreign investment constrain Addis Ababa's policy space even as it seeks greater control of minerals and infrastructure.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Mining and infrastructure concessions
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese and other minerals while renegotiating the balance between state participation and foreign operators. Chinese and other external firms remain important to logistics, financing, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues support state capacity but leave sovereignty exposed to foreign operators, price volatility, and offshore investment decisions.

highlights: Port and fisheries sovereignty remain exposed

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked security and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional connectivity, security cooperation, and access around its narrow territory. This supports stability but limits independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign access to fisheries and port commerce
frictionVectors.details: Weak monitoring capacity creates risks of illicit or opaque fishing arrangements and leakage of maritime value to foreign operators. Port modernization and trade finance also depend substantially on external partners.

highlights: Gold remains the core sovereignty asset
Debt recovery is constraining policy space

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control and illicit mining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is pressing for stronger state oversight and domestic value retention, but illegal mining, environmental damage, and entrenched commercial networks continue to erode resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals and energy financing
frictionVectors.details: Lithium ambitions and offshore oil development attract foreign capital while fiscal pressures and debt restructuring narrow Accra's bargaining room over ownership, processing, and infrastructure terms.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project offers transformational revenue but depends on large foreign-backed rail and port infrastructure. The state must balance participation and local-content demands against the financing and technical power of multinational consortia.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite concentration and concession politics
frictionVectors.details: Guinea's fiscal position remains heavily tied to foreign-operated bauxite exports. Regulatory uncertainty and opaque renegotiation risk could increase state control while discouraging diversification and domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and the state vulnerable to foreign buyers, price swings, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port, security, and illicit-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and political instability make port infrastructure and maritime routes vulnerable to opaque foreign deals, trafficking networks, and external political influence.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Terms
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and large Chinese and Gulf-backed infrastructure obligations constrain Nairobi's policy space. Debate over asset concessions and revenue guarantees remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional actors for port access, logistics corridors, and mineral supply chains creates pressure to balance investment with sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: South Africa remains the dominant buyer, financier, and infrastructure partner for Lesotho's strategic water exports. Revenue and construction disputes expose the kingdom to asymmetrical bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial Dependence on External Markets
frictionVectors.details: The textile sector depends heavily on foreign investors and preferential access to United States and regional markets. Energy imports and limited domestic generation further narrow sovereign room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore and Gold Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining firms dominate capital-intensive projects, while the government faces pressure to improve fiscal terms, local processing, and community benefits. Weak enforcement capacity limits effective national control.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport and Regional Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and proposed transport corridors attract Gulf, Chinese, and Western interest. Financing and concession structures could improve connectivity but risk long-term revenue leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest budget allocation, production decisions, and access to the central bank and National Oil Corporation. Periodic blockades keep exports vulnerable to domestic coercion.

frictionVectors.title: External Military and Energy Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain competing security and energy interests. Their involvement reinforces fragmented sovereignty around bases, contracts, and migration routes.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Resource-Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects rely heavily on foreign capital and offshore markets. The state faces recurring pressure to balance tax revenue and jobs against environmental damage and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, Energy, and External Finance
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf investors, and Western lenders compete for influence through port, energy, and transport projects. Weak electricity and road networks reduce Madagascar's ability to negotiate from strength.

highlights: Mining and power reforms seek new capital

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign investors for uranium, rare earths and niobium while regulatory capacity and local value capture remain limited. External financing needs increase bargaining pressure on the government.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND FUEL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and reliance on imported fuel expose Malawi to infrastructure bottlenecks and external lenders. New generation projects may improve supply but could deepen dependence on foreign operators and guarantees.

highlights: Junta tightens control over gold sector
Russian security partnership replaces Western role

frictionVectors.title: GOLD NATIONALIZATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is asserting greater state participation and revenue control over industrial gold mining, generating disputes with international operators. Production and investment risks are rising as contract terms are renegotiated.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security forces expands military autonomy from Western partners but creates political and financial dependence on Moscow. Persistent insurgency continues to threaten transport corridors and mining zones.

highlights: Iron ore logistics remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: SENEGAL GAS COORDINATION
frictionVectors.details: The shared offshore gas project with Senegal offers Mauritania new export leverage but requires sustained bilateral coordination over revenue, operations and maritime security. Delays or disputes could weaken expected fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND RAIL BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore revenues remain dependent on foreign capital, port access and the long rail corridor from inland mines to the Atlantic. Chinese and other external partners are important to expansion, limiting Mauritania's operational autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND DIEGO GARCIA
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains intertwined with the future of the Diego Garcia base and broader Indian Ocean security. Negotiations require balancing national claims with British and US strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: IMPORT AND CABLE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius depends heavily on imported fuel, food and maritime connectivity, including undersea communications infrastructure. Disruptions or intensified India-China competition could raise costs and narrow strategic room for maneuver.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables strengthen state leverage
Western Sahara remains a sovereignty multiplier

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses infrastructure, fisheries, phosphates and renewable-energy projects in Western Sahara to consolidate territorial control and attract recognition. The policy continues to generate opposition from Algeria, the Polisario Front and legal challengers.

frictionVectors.title: WATER AND ENERGY SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Severe water stress and dependence on imported hydrocarbons constrain Morocco despite rapid solar, wind and desalination investment. Foreign technology, financing and interconnection projects remain essential to scaling sovereign capacity.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains a Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Projects
frictionVectors.details: Major gas developments remain dependent on international capital, technology, and security guarantees, limiting Maputo's bargaining power despite expected export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant attacks continue to threaten energy infrastructure and civilian authority, while foreign military support remains central to protecting strategic areas.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries could strengthen national revenues, but production-sharing terms and foreign operator dominance will test Namibia's ability to retain value.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed projects promise industrial diversification but risk creating export enclaves unless local procurement, electricity access, and fiscal returns are secured.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and deeper security ties with Russia have increased regime autonomy but reduced access to established intelligence, logistics, and development networks.

frictionVectors.title: Export Corridor Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Border closures, regional pressure, and insecurity threaten uranium and crude-oil export routes, constraining the junta's ability to convert resource nationalism into stable revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Production Losses
frictionVectors.details: Sabotage, theft, and weak security continue to reduce crude output and fiscal receipts, leaving the state dependent on foreign operators and costly remediation.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Refinery, power, and transport expansion is attracting external capital, but debt exposure and concession terms remain politically sensitive as Abuja seeks greater domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Linked Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security role and mineral-trading position remain under intense scrutiny over alleged links to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, creating sanctions and diplomatic risks.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing greater domestic processing and infrastructure control, but budget support, foreign investment, and donor relationships still constrain strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration dependence
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore blocks attract foreign energy firms, but limited discoveries and weak domestic capacity constrain Sao Tome and Principe's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: External financing and investment are important for ports, fisheries, and maritime surveillance, creating exposure to creditor and strategic competition.

highlights: Oil and gas revenue governance tested

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government's push to review oil, gas, and mining arrangements strengthens its sovereignty narrative but risks investor uncertainty and disputes with international operators.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign financing and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure and energy projects remain dependent on external capital, including Gulf, Chinese, European, and multilateral partners, limiting policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign access to fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on foreign fleets and tuna-processing links, making licensing, labor, and value-capture arrangements persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian, European, Chinese, and other partners support maritime security and infrastructure, while Victoria seeks to avoid becoming dependent on any single power.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concentration
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mining operations generate export revenue but leave the state exposed to foreign capital, commodity cycles, and uneven domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, logistics, and transport projects are vital to mineral exports, creating leverage over national infrastructure and fiscal priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Security and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: International security assistance and foreign-backed port investments remain essential as Mogadishu struggles to consolidate control over territory, customs, and maritime assets.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Oil licensing, fisheries, and maritime boundaries attract external actors while federal-regional disputes and tensions involving Somaliland complicate unified resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral investment leverage
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater local processing of platinum-group metals, manganese and rare-earth inputs, while foreign firms retain substantial influence over capital, technology and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Power and freight bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability has improved from crisis levels, but Eskom debt and constrained rail and port capacity continue to weaken sovereign control over mineral supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese pipelines and Port Sudan to monetize its oil, leaving revenue and exports vulnerable to conflict, transit bargaining and infrastructure damage.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external patrons
frictionVectors.details: Regional governments, Chinese-linked oil interests and international donors shape security and resource decisions, limiting Juba's room for autonomous policy.

highlights: Gold and ports anchor external competition

frictionVectors.title: Gold war economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold extraction and export networks help finance rival armed factions, with foreign traders and regional intermediaries benefiting from weak oversight and opaque routes.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access contest
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and prospective naval or logistics arrangements has attracted competing regional and global interests while the civil war disrupts national infrastructure.

highlights: LNG and rail corridors reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining power
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over the long-delayed liquefied natural gas project expose tensions between Tanzania's demands for domestic value capture and the financing and technology requirements of international energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed rail and port infrastructure strengthens Tanzania's connectivity, but debt, concession terms and competition with alternative regional corridors remain sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major trade and transshipment hub, but reliance on foreign shipping, finance and logistics operators limits domestic control over strategic infrastructure revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel are pressuring northern Togo, increasing dependence on external security cooperation and threatening transport corridors linking the coast to landlocked neighbors.

highlights: Energy and phosphate sovereignty remain constrained

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and finance leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding and market access remain tied to migration control and macroeconomic cooperation, limiting Tunisian policy autonomy. Domestic resistance to perceived external conditionality is growing.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported hydrocarbons and electricity-system vulnerability while pursuing renewable projects that may bring external ownership and financing pressures.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The Lake Albert oil project and export pipeline remain central to Uganda's fiscal strategy but face international environmental pressure and dependence on foreign capital, contractors, and insurers.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external lenders retain influence over major transport and energy assets, while debt-service demands could narrow Kampala's room to negotiate resource and infrastructure terms.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt projects are drawing Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional investors, giving Lusaka leverage but also raising risks of opaque concessions, tax competition, and limited local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Transport-corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper exports depend heavily on external rail, port, and border corridors through Tanzania, Namibia, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe. Corridor disruptions can quickly weaken Zambia's bargaining position.

highlights: Gold and platinum remain externally intermediated

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals ownership
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, while Harare seeks beneficiation and tighter export controls without sufficient domestic finance or processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Power and sanctions constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and restricted access to international finance raise operating costs across mining and agriculture. External sanctions and reliance on regional power imports continue to limit sovereign policy space.
